lines.text: This autumn, A.I. learned to make video.
Claude Opus five point five writes motion design the way it writes software. A prompt becomes a launch film. Video became code.
But A.I. code got tests. A.I. video got vibes. Someone scrubs the timeline, says looks good, and ships it.
And the wordmark lands under the Reels buttons. The price shows up a second late. The caption runs off the square cut.
Everyone uses Kane C.L.I. to test their code. But testing is about to leave the codebase. When agents make what we ship, someone has to check what the code makes.
You write a storyboard. Shots, timecodes, exact copy, platform rules. One click.
Claude Code composes it in Remotion, while Kane reads the same storyboard and designs the tests. Twenty-four acceptance criteria, each cited to a line.
Then Kane judges. Every criterion, on every cut, frame by frame, in a real browser.
Claude's draft looked finished. Kane disagreed. On the vertical cut, the wordmark sits in the bottom band, right where TikTok draws its buttons. Frames six to nine. Fail.

So Claude can't stop. Claude Code's stop hook hands every attempt back to Kane, and Kane's verdict becomes the reason. Claude moves the wordmark, tries again, and Kane re-checks what failed. Then everything.
Sixty-two of sixty-two. And nothing is hidden. Every Claude session, every Kane command, the exact conditions, and the frames Kane saw.
Before, and after. When the cut is final, Kane runs its own tests, and proves every criterion.
About one credit per check. A targeted re-check, five.
Kane made code testable. Now it proves what the code makes.
